blogs.title: When an Expert’s Mapping Collapses: Finesse Wireless and the Federal Circuit’s Limits on Salvaging Jury Verdicts
blogs.description: This post would examine the court’s reversal on the ’134 patent as an evidentiary decision, not just a technical one. It would focus on the panel’s insistence that infringement must be proven through a clear element-by-element mapping at trial, and that a district court cannot reconstruct a coherent theory from scattered and contradictory expert testimony after the fact. The post would connect the opinion to Johns Hopkins v. Datascope and explore what it means for JMOL practice, expert preparation, and appellate review of patent verdicts.

blogs.title: Three Signals, Two Inputs, No Disclaimer: The Federal Circuit’s Narrow View of Prosecution-Based Surrender
blogs.description: This post would analyze the ’775 patent’s claim-construction issue and the court’s refusal to find clear disavowal even though the applicant amended the claims from “two or three signals” to “three signals.” It would explore the tension between numeric claim language and prosecution-history disclaimer doctrine, emphasizing the panel’s demand for a clear and unambiguous surrender before limiting claim scope. The post would be especially relevant for prosecutors and litigators dealing with amendments made to distinguish prior art on multiple grounds.

blogs.title: Seven Multiplications Means Seven: Algorithmic Exactness in Proving Infringement of Signal-Processing Patents
blogs.description: This post would focus on the court’s treatment of the accused radios’ mathematical operations under the ’775 patent. The key theme would be the Federal Circuit’s insistence that claimed digital operations—here, seven specified third-order multiplications—must be shown with precision, and that modulus and complex-conjugate operations cannot simply be waved into equivalence with the claimed products. The post would situate the decision within broader trends in software, DSP, and telecom patent litigation, where infringement increasingly turns on exact computational correspondence rather than high-level functional similarity.

blogs.title: How a $166 Million Patent Verdict Vanished: Rule 50, Waiver, and the Federal Circuit’s Appetite for Technical JMOL
blogs.description: This post would take a procedural and institutional angle on the case, using the reversal of the entire verdict and vacatur of damages to show how vulnerable large jury awards remain on appeal in technically dense patent suits. It would discuss the interaction among Rule 50 preservation, the district court’s waiver ruling on the “unique signals” argument, and the Federal Circuit’s ability to affirm or reverse on narrower sufficiency grounds. More broadly, it would ask whether Finesse Wireless reflects a continuing pattern of aggressive appellate scrutiny of Eastern District of Texas patent verdicts when the infringement theory depends on complex expert testimony.
